Breaking: US science academy urges journals to fix errors more promptly

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J.
  • Industry observers note that science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds.
  • Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J. Richards/AFP via Getty.

Industry observers note that science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds. Standards for fixing errors are also inconsistently applied across research journals, it says.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.

There are no data on how long retraction or correction presently takes, as journals do not generally disclose when they were alerted to a problem in a paper; the NASEM report says they should. On average, according to the Retraction Watch database, retractions occur around 2.4 years after a paper is published. The report recommends that editorial review processes be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months — at least when editors are looking at concerns over a single paper.

In a recent development, “The substantial picture is, the process is too slow,” says Randy Schekman, a cell biologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who chaired the 14-person committee that produced the NASEM report. A prompter and more transparent process would strengthen the reliability of the scientific record, he says.

The report was due to be published online on 19 November, but publication was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained some references with fabricated first names for authors, a possible sign that large language models had been used to write or edit the material and had been insufficiently checked.

“It's unfortunate that there were these flawed references in a report about fixing the literature,” says Jennifer Byrne, a cancer researcher and research integrity sleuth at the University of Sydney who first flagged the concern to Science when reviewing the report, which was shared ahead of publication with media outlets.

In a recent development, the report had two main aims: to speed up the process of retraction or correction and to lower the “tremendous emotional barriers” for authors to correct honest mistakes in the record, Schekman claims. “Part of the problem is that it’s too rare for a paper to be retracted,” he adds.

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Recent findings suggest that the report also suggests that journals shouldn’t just wait for complaints to reach them, but instead “take proactive steps” to identify errors and integrity problems. That might include journal-wide audits, or regularly monitoring social media and online platforms where post-publication issues are raised, it indicates.

Existing guidelines for publishers, such as those from the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in London, only urge a “timely” response to concerns without setting out expected schedules, and don’t suggest journals scan online platforms for complaints.

Recent findings suggest that “A major theme running through the report is that we have to distinguish between retraction or correction, and research misconduct,” notes Dorothy Bishop, a research-integrity sleuth in Oxford, UK, who was on the NASEM committee. Authors shouldn’t associate retracting a paper with the stigma of misconduct, she says. And although journal editors sometimes wait for a university to investigate whether there is research misconduct before correcting a paper, they shouldn’t, she adds.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a newly introduced record.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a newly introduced record.

In a recent development, calls for changing these attitudes aren’t newly introduced: journals have long emphasized that retractions can cover honest mistakes. When it comes to journal processes, Holden Thorpe, the editor in chief of Science, urged that issuing corrections or retractions and making a determination of misconduct be separated in an editorial in 2022, and COPE guidelines already emphasize the point. But “there are still plenty of people who see a correction or retraction as an allegation of fraud,” indicates Thorpe, who was also on the NASEM committee. “Hopefully, this report will accelerate the recognition of the distinction,” he says.

Tech Report: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago.
  • As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps.
  • To help solve this problem, Thomas A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering new evidence of ancient life.

To help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a fresh tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life.

In a recent development, to build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Recent findings suggest that using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced latest scientific information.

Industry observers note that the researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill important gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding.

The analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

Sources indicate that the greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

According to recent reports, to help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries.

By highlighting regions where important evidence may still be waiting, the newly introduced approach could help paleontologists plan more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable upcoming discoveries," states SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

According to recent reports, "But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically.".

#105166. Latest Update: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1047 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection.
  • Scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses.
  • Recent findings suggest that most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. Newly introduced research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

Scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to fresh threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

Recent findings suggest that most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage.

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

In a recent development, using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

In a recent development, according to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved.".

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an vital role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

Sources indicate that these structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

According to recent reports, as a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to fresh challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

"The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," indicates Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state.".

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage.

Recent findings suggest that after identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

Industry observers note that the results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

Sources indicate that this finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

"Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with latest challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications.

In a recent development, the findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise important questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

The research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

Industry observers note that "The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society.".

#105165. 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1234 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife.
  • The evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago.
  • Industry observers note that now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife. The discovery sheds new light on a disturbing burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove.

The evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he noticed that unusually large numbers of people had been buried around the kings. He suspected that these individuals had been sacrificed following their rulers' deaths, but he could not identify physical evidence of fatal injuries.

Industry observers note that now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied. The findings provide compelling upcoming support for the theory that human sacrifice played a role in the burial traditions of ancient Egypt's first kings.

"I was drawn to these retainers partly because, even though they were buried around royalty, they are mostly relegated to footnotes in the grander narrative," said Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University, who led the research published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. Campbell is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press).

"Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death?".

A 5,000-Year-Old Mystery Surrounding Egypt's First Kings.

According to recent reports, around 3000 BCE, the earliest kings of a unified Egypt constructed elaborate burial complexes at Abydos. These sites included royal tombs, additional burial chambers, and enclosed areas believed to have been used for funeral ceremonies.

It has been revealed that surrounding the main structures were numerous smaller graves arranged in rows. Some royal burial sites were accompanied by hundreds of these subsidiary burials, raising questions about why so many people had been buried in close association with a single ruler.

"Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others," remarked Campbell. "Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or mid-level officials as well as artisans.".

The extraordinary concentration of graves led Petrie to propose that the people buried alongside the kings were victims of a practice known as retainer sacrifice.

"Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies," explained Campbell. "In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler's power. Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced.".

Despite the suspicious circumstances, Petrie could not find convincing evidence that the individuals had died violently. Without identifiable fatal injuries, the possibility of human sacrifice remained an unresolved archaeological mystery.

Campbell decided to revisit the original excavation evidence, hoping that modern forensic techniques could reveal clues that had escaped investigators a century earlier.

Modern Forensics Reveals Evidence of Violent Deaths.

Although Petrie documented his excavations carefully, he eventually reburied most of the human remains. He did, however, preserve a selection of skulls, some of which were transferred to the United Kingdom.

Campbell located 46 of these skulls in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University and examined them using contemporary forensic knowledge.

Sources indicate that the results revealed injuries that had previously gone unrecognized. Eighteen skulls demonstrated substantial cranial trauma, primarily in the form of linear fractures. Petrie had apparently interpreted these cracks as damage caused by natural processes rather than injuries sustained by living people.

According to recent reports, modern forensic methods made it possible to identify the fractures as perimortem injuries, meaning they occurred around the time of death. Their characteristics suggest that some of the individuals may have suffered deliberate, potentially fatal blows to the head.

"The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death," said Campbell, who also reported evidence of sharp-force trauma on some of the 18 skulls, including a chopping injury to one individual's eye.

These findings suggest that at least 39% of the examined individuals may have been deliberately killed, providing key upcoming evidence in support of the long-standing human sacrifice hypothesis.

How Were Ancient Egypt's Royal Attendants Killed?

Although the skull injuries offer strong evidence of violence, the precise circumstances of the deaths remain uncertain.

According to recent reports, ancient Egyptian artwork frequently portrays kings striking enemies with maces, but Campbell noted that the royal attendants buried at Abydos were not enemy combatants. The injuries also do not match the damage typically associated with these weapons.

Industry observers note that A mace would generally produce depressed skull fractures, while the injuries identified in this study were predominantly linear. Such fractures are more commonly associated with impacts from broad, flat objects or severe falls.

Accidental falls cannot be entirely excluded. However, a fall powerful enough to fracture the skull would likely have caused injuries elsewhere in the skeleton. Such damage should have appeared in Petrie's excavation records or photographs, yet no corresponding evidence was documented.

Sources indicate that the researchers also cannot determine how the remaining individuals died. Some may have died naturally, while others could have been killed using methods that left no recognizable marks on their bones, such as asphyxiation.

According to recent reports, additional injuries might also have been found if the rest of their skeletons were available for examination. Unfortunately, most of those remains were reburied more than a century ago, leaving researchers with only part of the physical evidence.

Ancient Skulls Reveal Upcoming Clues to Egypt's Dark Past.

It has been revealed that the findings demonstrate how archaeological collections can preserve notable clues long after their original excavation. Even when evidence is incomplete, advances in scientific techniques can provide new answers to questions that earlier researchers were unable to resolve.

For Campbell, the possibility of locating and examining the remaining skeletal material offers an especially intriguing opportunity to learn more about the people buried around Egypt's earliest kings.

"If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them!" noted Campbell. "Still, this study highlights how much new information about the past can be revealed when we revisit previous data armed with updated methods and knowledge, even for datasets that are incomplete and imperfect like this one.".

Robins ‘aims for the stars’ as Stoke dream of Premier League return

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Championship’s form side climbed to second after holding on resiliently with 10 men to knock Birmingham off the summit.
  • This time last year, with Christmas on the near horizon, Stoke sat second in the Championship table and were beginning to wonder whether they might allow themselves to dream.
  • Industry observers note that experience has taught the benefit of pragmatism, so no one will be getting ahead of themselves just yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Championship’s form side climbed to second after holding on resiliently with 10 men to knock Birmingham off the summit.

There have been false dawns before. Plenty of them. This time last year, with Christmas on the near horizon, Stoke sat second in the Championship table and were beginning to wonder whether they might allow themselves to dream. So hopeless was their subsequent run that by the onset of spring they were forced to consider a potential relegation fight.

Industry observers note that experience has taught the benefit of pragmatism, so no one will be getting ahead of themselves just yet. But this weekend was supposed to be the massive test for Mark Robins’s team and few considered they would pass it quite so resoundingly.

Facing a Birmingham side who arrived top of the table and with firmly held Premier League ambitions, Stoke dominated for an hour, the hitherto goal-shy George Hirst earning a well-deserved lead to send a bumper crowd into raptures. The hand-wringing that then followed Luca Bombino’s sending-off with half an hour remaining made the victory that followed all the sweeter. The 10 men of Stoke were superb. It was no surprise that it took considerable time to convince those in the stands to depart for home after the final whistle.

In a recent development, you see, it is not just that Stoke are second in the table, kept off top spot by goal difference. It is not even that they are undoubtedly the Championship’s form side, with just one defeat in their past 13 games. It is the whole feeling around the place; the resilience Robins has developed, and the belief that they can take on the significant guns and beat them.

“We are a work in progress, but today was that step in quality against different opponents. A step up in class,” stated Robins. “I thought we were really, really good. The intensity, bravery and the intent that we highlighted was everything that we asked for.

It has been revealed that “And, on the back of that, you’ve got the support that are absolutely right behind us. They trust the players. That is a really good feeling. It’s a great feeling for the players. It’s a heady mix, really.”.

Sources indicate that eight years have passed since Stoke were last in the top flight; eight years spent as the Championship equivalent of a sea sponge, doing the bare minimum to survive and letting defeats wash over them while remaining resolutely attached to the rocks of the bottom half of the table. During that time they have ended every campaign no higher than 14th and no lower than 18th. Now, something altogether different is afoot. And this may well be the win that convinces supporters to trust their upbeat instincts.

Sources indicate that there was an unavoidable fact heading into Saturday’s game. Stoke’s four defeats this season had all come when tasked with opponents fighting at the top end of the table in Swansea, Southampton, Wolves and Middlesbrough. They had shown themselves capable against much of the division, but a failure to deliver against another Championship heavyweight would have raised legitimate questions about their realistic aspirations.

The three August defeats at the start of the campaign preceded the departure of their best player, Sorba Thomas. His replacement, Jack McGlynn, has been an inspired signing. That this victory came without the talismanic figure of Ethan Galbraith, who was absent through illness, is considerable.

As well as switching to a three-man defence following those season-opening losses, a key factor in their upturn has been the restoration of a touch of old-school Stoke; a physicality that was frequently evident on a cold Saturday afternoon.

Recent findings suggest that bobby Madley, the referee, did not always take kindly to such an approach – to the indignation of the home crowd, who frequently made their feelings clear – but there was no complaint over Bombino’s sending-off for a second yellow after a rash challenge that left him head in hands before the card had even been shown. Tears followed on his slow trudge towards the tunnel, but he need not have worried, with Birmingham barely threatening thereafter.

Industry observers note that given just five points separate the top eight in the Championship table, it would come as no great shock to see Stoke drop off at some point. They do not have the financial benefit of recent Premier League parachute payments or substantial-spending owners, they are not prolific goalscorers, and a look at their expected goals and expected points tallies shows them firmly in the bottom half of the table. But they are finding ways to win and if McGlynn has a habit of scoring from unexpectedly long distances, perhaps it is because he is good at it.

Recent findings suggest that before this weekend, Robins had revealed that a top-eight finish was the pre-season target. “You aim for the stars and hopefully you land trying to grab hold of one,” he had mentioned, rather poetically.

According to recent reports, if promotion is a “P” they dare not yet speak of, another one – playoffs – is becoming an increasingly realistic proposition. No more sticking to a rock. Swim free and prosper.

Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine.
  • The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful upcoming way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline.
  • Sources indicate that to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine. The same approach can also identify people whose brains show exceptional resistance to cognitive decline, suggesting they may eventually become "super agers.".

The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful upcoming way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline. Unlike conventional biomarkers, these patterns of brain activity might eventually be possible to change through targeted interventions.

Sources indicate that to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum. One group had Alzheimer's disease, while the other consisted of super agers, older individuals whose memories remained comparable to those of people decades younger. Using the differences between these groups, the scientists created a scoring system to evaluate brain activity in cognitively healthy adults between 55 and 70.

According to recent reports, the results revealed a striking connection between brain activity and future cognitive health. People whose brain patterns more closely resembled those of Alzheimer's patients were more likely to experience cognitive decline, accumulate amyloid-beta plaques, and receive an Alzheimer's diagnosis during follow-up periods extending up to 12 years. Those with activity patterns resembling super agers were more likely to maintain their cognitive abilities and avoid these outcomes.

A New Way to Detect Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss.

It has been revealed that the latest scoring system predicted future cognitive decline more effectively than several established indicators, including demographic characteristics, genetic risk factors, and amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers. This suggests that examining how different regions of the brain communicate could reveal Alzheimer's risk earlier than existing approaches.

"We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer's field nowadays -- most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease," mentioned Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and senior author of the study. "What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.".

Industry observers note that zhang envisions a future in which treatments could potentially move someone's brain activity toward the patterns associated with greater cognitive resilience. Possible approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity.

Industry observers note that transcranial magnetic stimulation has already demonstrated potential for changing brain activity in people being treated for depression. However, neither of these proposed approaches has been tested in this context for preventing cognitive decline, and researchers do not yet know whether changing brain activity would alter the course of Alzheimer's disease. The fresh findings provide a starting point for identifying which brain regions might be useful treatment targets.

Industry observers note that "There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it," Zhang said. "That's why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component -- so we know what a good pattern should be.".

What Makes Super Agers' Brains Different?

Depending on how they are defined, approximately 10% of older adults may qualify as super agers. For this research, the term referred to people at least 75 years old who performed on memory tests at a level typical of a 45-year-old while maintaining normal executive function for their age.

Industry observers note that scientists have become increasingly interested in these unusually resilient individuals. Most earlier studies, however, compared super-agers with other older adults who performed normally on cognitive assessments.

According to recent reports, zhang recognized that this approach could overlook crucial biological differences. Two people might receive similar scores on memory tests despite having very different underlying brain health. One might already be developing amyloid-beta plaques or showing other biological changes associated with aging, while the other might not.

"Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities," he mentioned. "Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.".

In other words, comparing super agers with a broad mixture of seemingly healthy older adults makes it difficult to determine which brain characteristics actually protect against decline.

According to recent reports, the Stanford team took a different approach. Rather than using typical older adults as the comparison group, they examined people with Alzheimer's disease who were approximately the same age as the super agers. This created two more clearly defined groups at opposite ends of the cognitive spectrum.

Brain Scans Reveal a Hidden Pattern.

The researchers drew on imaging information collected through several major research initiatives, including the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

Industry observers note that they examined resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 super agers and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. This imaging technique records patterns of brain activity while a person lies quietly inside a scanner.

The comparison uncovered distinctive differences in activity across multiple brain regions. Some areas indicated greater activity while others showed reduced activity, producing recognizable patterns that distinguished the two groups. Scientists refer to the relationships among these regions as functional connectivity, or the functional connectome.

Industry observers note that using these patterns, the team developed a measurement called the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome, or ARC score. This scoring method distinguished super agers from Alzheimer's patients with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers then investigated whether the same brain signature could help predict what would happen to people who had not yet developed any noticeable cognitive problems.

Predicting Alzheimer's Risk Years in Advance.

It has been revealed that the team applied the ARC scoring system to more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults between the ages of 55 and 70. Their scores fell across a broad range, with lower values reflecting brain activity more similar to super agers and higher values indicating patterns closer to those observed in Alzheimer's patients.

At the beginning of the study, people with high and low ARC scores highlighted no obvious differences in cognitive performance. As researchers examined follow-up data collected over subsequent years, however, important differences became apparent.

"We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease," stated Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry and lead author of the study.

The available follow-up periods differed across the datasets. Some participants had records extending as long as 12 years, although most were tracked for approximately five to six years. Even within these shorter periods, the initial ARC scores helped predict subsequent changes in cognitive abilities.

Industry observers note that people whose scores indicated more Alzheimer's-like brain activity experienced more rapid declines on standard tests of memory, attention, and executive function. In contrast, those with patterns most similar to super agers generally experienced the slowest cognitive decline.

It has been revealed that "We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," Zhao said. "Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.".

A More Precise Measure of Brain Aging.

The team also investigated how ARC scores related to another measure of neurological health called brain age. This measure estimates brain aging using functional MRI information collected from healthy individuals.

Although the two measurements showed some correlation, Zhang emphasized that ARC provides more targeted information about a person's vulnerability or resistance to cognitive decline during aging.

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," he mentioned.

The findings suggest that patterns of communication between brain regions may offer valuable information about future cognitive health that cannot be captured through standard memory testing alone.

They also raise the possibility that combining brain activity measurements with established Alzheimer's biomarkers could improve the identification of people who would benefit most from earlier monitoring or future preventive treatments.

Could Brain Training Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that ARC scores are not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. For now, the system should be viewed as a potential tool for tracking cognitive health and estimating future risk.

In a recent development, zhang also stresses that a person's score is not a permanent prediction of their future. Brain activity can change over time, and an individual who initially indicates a resilient pattern may not maintain it indefinitely.

For example, the proportion of people with super-ager-like ARC scores generally declines with advancing age. Brain injuries and neuropsychiatric conditions can also influence the patterns associated with cognitive resilience.

It has been revealed that importantly, this potential for change may work in both directions. If brain activity can shift toward patterns associated with vulnerability, Zhang hopes future treatments might also encourage it to move toward greater resilience.

His research team is preparing a trial that will measure ARC scores before and after cognitive training. The goal is to explore whether targeted training can influence the brain activity patterns associated with healthier cognitive aging.

"But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage," he mentioned. "That's why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer's-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I'm optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies.".

Although it remains unknown whether modifying these brain patterns can prevent or delay Alzheimer's, the discovery offers a potentially important latest direction for research. By identifying differences in brain activity before symptoms emerge, scientists may eventually gain a valuable opportunity to intervene while cognitive function is still intact.

Researchers from Children's National Hospital; the University of Texas at Austin; Lehigh University; Penn State College of Medicine; Newly introduced York University Grossman School of Medicine; and the University of California, Los Angeles also participated in the research.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer's Association grant, and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

Breaking: Nonprofit Common Space will launch 1st 'humanitarian satellite' in 2027

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan.
  • The nonprofit Common Space looks to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites, whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world.
  • Recent findings suggest that that plan firmed up a bit today (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan.

The nonprofit Common Space looks to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites, whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world.

Recent findings suggest that that plan firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space unveiled the builder of the first of those satellites: Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence manufacturer.

There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space.

The nonprofit wants to change that via its envisioned constellation, which it claims will collect imagery specifically for humanitarian and public-interest purposes. Common Space plans to operate on a "club-good model," which will share infrastructure and costs across a large community, allowing extensive, low-cost access to high-quality imagery.

Satellogic is now officially part of this picture.

It has been revealed that "With Satellogic as our spacecraft partner, we're moving from vision to orbit and putting high-resolution data into the hands of those who need it most," Common Space co-founder Rhiannan Price said in a statement today. "This isn't just another satellite. We're building infrastructure to serve people for years to come.".

The satellite is Satellogic's NewSat Mark V, which Common Space selected after a competitive request-for-proposal process.

The NewSat Mark V is just 32 inches (82 centimeters) long and weighs 85 pounds (38.5 kilograms) here on Earth. But the microsatellite packs a great deal of capability into that small package. From low Earth orbit (LEO), it naturally resolves features on the ground as small as 27.5 inches (70 cm), which Satellogic's proprietary algorithms can boost to a "super resolution" of 19.7 inches (50 cm).

Recent findings suggest that the satellite is scheduled to launch in July 2027, on a rocket that has yet to be announced. Satellogic will handle the preparations for that launch and manage satellite operations, which are expected to last at least five years in LEO. The company has extensive experience with such work; it has flown 61 of its Earth-observing satellites to date, all of which deployed successfully.

And Satellogic is aligned with Common Space philosophically, the organization stressed.

"Common Space shares our belief that persistent global intelligence shouldn't be reserved for a few. Humanitarian responders and journalists are often first on the ground and last to get access, yet they need frequent, high-resolution imagery to see what's really happening so they can act with confidence," Luciano Giesso, vice president of space systems at Satellogic, said in the same statement. "This mission puts our vision of democratized access into practice.".

Industry observers note that common Space is at the moment raising money to expand the constellation to six satellites, which it hopes to have in place by 2030. This will allow daily high-resolution coverage of "priority areas," according to the nonprofit.

In a recent development, editor's note: The original version of this story stated that the first Satellogic satellite will launch on a SpaceX rocket. This information was in an embargoed version of today's press release but was not in the final version, so it has been removed from this story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Messi booked for throwing ball into opponent’s face.

Columbus coach insists Argentine deserved red card.

Defending champions thrashed 3-0 in series opener.

Columbus Crew coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have been sent off after throwing a ball into an opponent’s face as Inter Miami crashed to a 3-0 defeat in the MLS Cup playoffs on Saturday.

Messi’s frustration boiled over on the stroke of half-time when he hurled a throw-in into the face of Columbus forward Gonzalo Tapia, with 10-man Miami trailing 1-0 at the time.

Messi and Tapia were both shown yellow cards for the incident by referee Allen Chapman, but Courtois remarked afterwards that the Argentina superstar should have been given a red card.

“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said at a post-game press conference when asked about the incident. “It’s just really sad.”.

Chapman later defended his decision to show Messi only a yellow card.

“The force used was negligible and the offense did not reach the level of violent conduct,” Chapman told a pool reporter.

Miami had already been reduced to 10 men when the incident occurred and were trailing 1-0 after an early penalty from the Chile international Tapia.

The reigning MLS champions went on to suffer a 3-0 defeat, with Taha Habroune doubling Columbus’s lead shortly after half-time before Tapia added his second at Miami’s Nu Stadium.

The result means seventh-seeded Columbus, the 2023 champions, can eliminate Messi and Miami from the playoffs with a victory in Game 2 of the best-of-three series in Ohio next Friday.

“It was a game where nothing went right for us, and we effectively created their chances for them,” Miami coach Kily González stated afterwards.

“We didn’t produce the great performance we had hoped for. Everything went wrong, but we have to learn from it because next time, if we don’t win, we’re out.

“There’s no better challenge for us as a team than this. It’s a test of character, and I know my team has that character.”.

Joaquín Valiente scored twice in the space of two minutes as FC Dallas beat the Portland Timbers 3-0 in the opening game of their best-of-three Western Conference first-round series.

The 25-year-old Uruguayan midfielder broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute, volleying home a rebound after Daniel Job’s shot was parried by Portland goalkeeper James Pantemis.

Valiente doubled the lead two minutes later, timing his run to meet another pass from Job before redirecting the ball between Pantemis’s legs.

Samuel Sarver completed the scoring in the fourth minute of stoppage time, finishing a cross from Logan Farrington on the counterattack.

Dallas goalkeeper Daniel de Sousa Britto, known simply as Daniel, made four saves, while Pantemis finished with five for Portland.

The Timbers also lost Ariel Lassiter to an apparent injury in the 33rd minute.

Second-seeded Dallas can advance to the Western Conference semi-finals with a victory in Portland next Saturday.

Teenager Peyton Miller scored one goal and helped create another as the New England Revolution beat the Philadelphia Union 2-0 in the opening game of their Eastern Conference first-round series.

The 19-year-old Miller became the fifth-youngest goalscorer in MLS Cup playoffs history when he volleyed home a cross from Jack Harrison in the 73rd minute, his effort bouncing off the crossbar and into the net.

Upcoming England had taken the lead in the 10th minute when Miller’s shot from the edge of the penalty area deflected off Philadelphia defender Nathan Harriel for an own goal.

Harrison, who came on as a substitute in the 62nd minute, was making his first appearance since 9 September after missing more than two months with a quadriceps injury.

Philadelphia nearly equalized in the 37th minute when Cavan Sullivan turned and fired a shot from outside the penalty area that struck the left post.

The Union fielded the youngest starting lineup in MLS Cup playoffs history, with an average age of 23 years and 207 days, breaking the record set by the Latest York Red Bulls in 2022.

Matt Turner made two saves to preserve the shutout for New England, who can advance to the Eastern Conference semi-finals with a victory in Philadelphia next Saturday.

#105154. A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.
  • According to recent reports, the object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C.
  • In a recent development, the discovery was announced at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.

According to recent reports, the object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Early estimates suggest it ranks among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If its status is confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets at the moment recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

In a recent development, the discovery was announced at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team. Holman made the initial discovery, while Jurić helped gather the additional evidence needed to verify it.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman stated. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach.".

Industry observers note that "Finding an object this major, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić remarked. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.".

How Astronomers Discovered the Hidden World.

According to recent reports, the breakthrough occurred on the evening of October 13, when Holman examined observations gathered by Rubin earlier in 2026. He was using specialized software developed with his colleague Kevin Napier to search for previously unidentified objects moving through the solar system.

The program compares billions of telescope detections, looking for individual points of light that appear in multiple observations and move in ways that suggest they belong to the same object. When the software identified ED138, Holman rapidly realized that its apparent brightness and enormous distance pointed to something unusually large.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman remarked. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.".

Recent findings suggest that to check the finding, Jurić examined Rubin's stored observations and located 20 additional detections of ED138, including some captured as early as March 2026. The researchers then searched historical records from other astronomical surveys and identified images of the object dating back to 2016.

Together, these observations allowed the team to reconstruct more than a decade of the distant world's orbital motion, strengthening the evidence that the discovery was genuine.

Could This Be Our Solar System's Sixth Dwarf Planet?

ED138 presently lies approximately 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One astronomical unit represents the average distance separating Earth and the Sun. By comparison, Pluto's average orbital distance is about 40 au.

It has been revealed that because ED138 travels beyond Neptune, astronomers classify it as a trans-Neptunian object (TNO). These distant bodies are valuable to scientists because their physical properties and orbital paths preserve clues about the solar system's distant past.

By examining their sizes, compositions, and movements, researchers can better understand how the solar system developed, how its giant planets shifted positions, and how smaller bodies were redistributed during that process.

Sources indicate that however, being a trans-Neptunian object does not automatically make ED138 a dwarf planet. An essential requirement is that the object's gravity must be strong enough to shape it into a nearly round body.

Using measurements of ED138's brightness and distance, along with estimates of how much sunlight its surface reflects, astronomers calculate that it could measure anywhere from 600 to 1,500 kilometers across.

An icy object within that size range would generally be expected to have enough gravity to become round. Nevertheless, scientists will need more observations to establish ED138's actual dimensions and determine whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet.

Why Such a Massive World Remained Undiscovered.

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is how an object this large managed to escape detection for so long.

ED138 occupies a region of the sky near the plane of the Milky Way, where millions of stars create an exceptionally crowded background. Against that dense field of light, the distant object's faint movement was difficult for earlier telescopes and surveys to distinguish.

Rubin Observatory has an vital advantage. Its ability to repeatedly observe the Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with advanced computer algorithms, makes it possible to search enormous quantities of astronomical data for subtle changes in the positions of objects.

In a recent development, by examining millions or even billions of individual light detections, these systems can recognize the movement of small solar system bodies that might otherwise disappear into the surrounding stars. This capability was essential to finding ED138 in such a challenging part of the sky.

Rubin Observatory Could Reveal More Hidden Worlds.

The newly identified object adds to a growing collection of solar system discoveries made by Rubin Observatory as it began gathering observations ahead of its ambitious Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which officially started in June 2026.

Even before the survey began, the observatory was producing remarkable results. In April, Rubin's solar system researchers reported observations of more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids, including approximately 380 fresh trans-Neptunian objects.

Sources indicate that the team described that enormous collection of discoveries as "the tip of the iceberg," anticipating that the full survey would uncover many more objects. The identification of ED138 offers an early indication of just how significant those future findings could be.

In a recent development, rubin's combination of extensive sky coverage, sensitivity, and rapid observations is also changing how astronomers investigate upcoming discoveries. Once an object has been identified, researchers can search older telescope images to find instances when it was photographed but went unrecognized.

According to recent reports, "Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision," Jurić said. "And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a upcoming object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and 'precover' objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.".

As Rubin continues surveying the southern sky over the next decade, astronomers expect its observations to uncover additional objects that previous searches missed, potentially revealing more large, icy worlds in the outer solar system.

Anyone interested in exploring ED138 can view its location and orbit using Orbitviewer, an interactive web-based application that displays the solar system in three dimensions and allows users to explore its structure in real time.

Operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

#105153. How a green economy could help reverse climate change

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

How a green economy could help reverse climate change

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable.
  • If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.
  • It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.

If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.

It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.

It has been revealed that its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and  recycling and reusing resources and raw materials.

"Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," said Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues, he published a major report in 2020 evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.

In principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.

Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.

Industry observers note that the economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japanand Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshore production is included.

Industry observers note that in the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.

But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.

In India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.

"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," mentioned Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.

And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.

These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry.

Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.

According to recent reports, there's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.

In a recent development, but that doesn't mean overall fewer resources are being used because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.

The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased, but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.

Global resource consumption has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear whether green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.

"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," noted Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.

She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.

"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need.".

Some researchers have concluded that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.

Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.

That applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life improve significantly.

Industry observers note that under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.

In a recent development, ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne revealed that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.

However, there is still no conclusive evidence that an entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.

Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead for a needs-based economy.

It has been revealed that "A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he said. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.

Today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life or environmental damage.

It has been revealed that "The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," mentioned Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

An analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to gross domestic product growth. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.

Countries face a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.

It has been revealed that and the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.

Sources indicate that achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is currently uncertain.".

This article was originally written in German.

#105152. Don Bluth on the future of animation and AI: Thats definitely a road I dont want to travel on
