General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly key role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections.
  • In a recent development, arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods.
  • Industry observers note that now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly key role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

In a recent development, arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Industry observers note that now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

In a recent development, the findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System.

The research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

In 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising vital questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

In a recent development, the latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this key protein.

According to recent reports, "Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," notes first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections.".

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon.".

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses.

To understand why arginine has such an vital effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

It has been revealed that the instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

It has been revealed that scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

It has been revealed that to investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she states.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System.

In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

Sources indicate that MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

Sources indicate that the reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

As a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

"These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids.".

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice.

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Sources indicate that mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses.

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Recent findings suggest that arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

Industry observers note that "Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful.".

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially key implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

According to recent reports, "Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie states. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come.".

The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed tech giant's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.
  • Reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the manufacturer nears completion of its fresh $2 billion plant here, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC.

The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed tech giant's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.

Reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases.

Keogh stated he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more key thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears.

"It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh noted during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell.".

It has been revealed that keogh said achieving an order book of 12 to 18 months "would be great" and is something he thinks the company can do before production. Scout on Thursday said plant construction is "in its final phase.".

Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, that include an internal combustion engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries.

Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the manufacturer to decide to offer EREVs as well.

Keogh remarked extended-range and SUV models are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs.

The CEO also stated the tech giant is drawing interest from its target markets, which include owners of off-road vehicles such as the Ford Bronco and Jeep Wrangler as well as full-size pickup trucks and U.S. EV leader Tesla.

It has been revealed that given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh said the manufacturer is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company plans to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models.

Recent findings suggest that both the Traveler and Terra are expected to start at under $60,000. The EREV models are expected to feature more than 500 miles of range, according to the firm, compared with 300 miles of range for the all-electric models.

According to recent reports, "The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh remarked. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through.".

His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry.

Keogh stated Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed.

Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra, which feature sleek, yet rugged, exteriors that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

Now this is a revelation to wig out over.

Industry observers note that sarah Michelle Gellar and Freddie Prinze Jr.’s paths didn’t officially cross until the late ‘90s on I Know What You Did Last Summer, but as they recently learned they had more in common than they realized. Specifically, a shared family experience that traces back decades before they graced the screen.

“We always joke that the closest connection I had to my husband's side of the family,” Gellar told E! News in an exclusive interview, “was that for a small time I went to the same high school that my husband's dad went to, and that was like sort of our one thing.”.

After all, though Gellar—mom to Charlotte, 17, and Rocky, 14, with Prinze—is a native Upcoming Yorker, her husband was born in Los Angeles and grew up in New Mexico. (His dad Freddie Prinze, however, hailed from New York.).

Industry observers note that she continued, “Then through Ancestry, we found out that our grandparents lived less than two miles away from each other in the Bronx at one point, which they could have potentially known each other. That's kind of crazy.”.

For the Buffy the Vampire Slayer star, who teamed up with Ancestry for its Gathering the Good initiative, it was an opportunity to explore her own family’s legacy while also looking at the spirit of giving through history. So, tracing how her loved ones made the journey to America in the 1890s at the same time philanthropist Lena Sittig space was creating what is now considered to be the modern toy drive, really hit home how interconnected the mission is.

Sources indicate that “I learned that my grandmother was coming over on a ship at 16 years old, right when Lena was having her idea for this,” she shared. “It’s kind of crazy how the world intertwines, and it just reminds you that you're just such a small part of such a bigger picture.”.

It’s especially poignant as diving back into her roots has not always been a focal point for Gellar.

“It's funny, I didn't really spend that much time thinking about my history and my ancestry because I try so hard to live in the moment,” she explained. “And when Ancestry came to me and talked about what they wanted to do, I thought, ‘What a great idea to be able to learn acts of kindness, acts of goodness that your family may have been a part of that you never knew.’”.

Sources indicate that as the Cruel Intentions alum knows, ‘tis the season to pay it forward. “The holiday season gets so dramatic—presents and all that,” she noted. “And I always look for what are the things that you could give someone that are really meaningful.”.

So, the 49-year-old posited, “What's more meaningful than learning about where you came from and your family and things you may not have known?”.

Industry observers note that to Gellar, it all comes back to Lena Sittig and her Brooklyn Christmas Tree Society, and how her idea is sparking change so many generations later. In fact, the Ringer actress teamed up with Ancestry to fulfill Christmas lists for Children’s Aid.

“So often, I think we think, ‘Well, I'm one person. What can I do?’ And then you see something like that, and you realize, oh wow, one person can do a lot,” she told E!. “But then to take it that step further, and maybe there's people in her family had no idea they were related to her.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Can you imagine going back in your history and finding out that one person in your family was responsible for millions of children's gifts all over the world because they had this idea?” Gellar added. “I think it's really special.”.

And it’s an experience Gellar wants to send far and wide, teasing what many of her loved ones—not to mention anyone looking to explore the impact their family has made on others—may be getting under the tree this year.

Recent findings suggest that “There's something for me about the how tangible it was,” she admitted. “I saw signatures, I saw writing. it makes it seem just much more real to you than just getting an email that says, ‘You know you came from here’ like, seeing their actual signatures at Ellis Island. It's also something too, growing up in Newly introduced York City, you forget about it. But this is the gateway.”.

Industry observers note that the moon shines close to the ringed giant Saturn after sunset tonight (Nov. 20), presenting a spectacular naked-eye display as the stars of the Great Square of Pegasus twinkle nearby.

Saturn's steady light will appear a little over 5 degrees from the 82%-lit moon in the southeastern sky after the sun dips below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length.

Moonlight will hide fainter stars from view, though you should be able to spot Algenib, Markab, Alpheratz and Scheat arrayed in a diamond formation above the lunar disk, marking out the asterism of the Great Square of Pegasus in the November sky.

According to recent reports, the moon will present a spectacular target through the eyepiece of a 6-inch telescope, as the terminator line separating night from day creeps ever closer to its western edge. It's a great time to explore the 110 km-wide Gassendi Crater on the edge of Mare Humorum as its eastern rim and central peaks throw intense shadows across its interior.

Slewing your telescope over to Saturn will reveal details and subtle variations in the cloud surface of the gas giant, along with its iconic ring system, which is gradually becoming more visible following its ring plane crossing in March 2025.

Depending on viewing conditions, you may also notice a shoal of bright, star-like points of light surrounding Saturn's disk, which represent the large moons Titan, Dione, Tethys, Rhea and Iapetus.

Nguyen Quynh Anh's reign as Miss Universe Vietnam has officially come to an end.

The beauty queen was initially suspended in October when private messages speaking negatively about other pageant participants became public, and now the organizers have revoked her title due to Nguyen's conduct while under suspension.

The complications occurred while Nguyen was barred from performing in all "artistic performance activities" related to Miss Universe for six months, the show’s organizers, Five6 Entertainment, announced in a Nov. 18 statement, according to Tuoi Tre News.

In addition to being suspended from events for the group text—which included runner-up Trinh My Anh—containing derogatory remarks about past winners, fellow contestants and judges, the model was ordered to pay a fine, the outlet said.

However, when the influencer attended a community event while banned from representing the pageant, the production company, per Tuoi Tre News, said her appearance caused concerns that "affected the image of Miss Universe Vietnam and its organizers.".

In addition to promoting her title while suspended, the organizers stated that the 27-year-old delayed signing her management contract in order to prioritize a "mental health condition" amid the transitional period. Still, the team noted they learned Nguyen signed an exclusive contract with a competitor management agency and "continued accepting performance engagements and attending events without reaching an agreement with Five6.".

In a recent development, in response to the initial backlash, the competition's runner-up, Trinh, apologized on Instagram. Meanwhile, Nguyen released an Oct. 13 statement transcribed by the outlet where she apologized "to the women concerned and everyone affected by this incident, especially the audience.".

Sources indicate that "I understand that holding a beauty queen title does not make me incapable of making mistakes," her statement continued. "However, the title requires me to be more mindful and careful about my words, conduct and responsibilities, even in seemingly minor matters.".

Recent findings suggest that E! News has reached out to Nguyen Quynh Anh regarding the recent conduct allegations but has not yet heard back.

The release noted that her title was formally revoked after reviewing the conditions of holding the crown, the outlet said.

It has been revealed that and given the unexpected exit, Vietnam will not send a competitor to the global Miss Universe finale on Nov. 24 in Puerto Rico.

#105103. El Niño Is Driving a Record Marine Heat Wave Off the California Coast

El Niño Is Driving a Record Marine Heat Wave Off the California Coast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface.
  • The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.
  • A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface. He’s never seen anything like what’s been coming back for the past few months, as a super El Niño fuels record heat off the California coast. The marine heat wave is affecting wildlife and helping to juice the record-setting storms hitting the state at the start of the rainy season.

The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.

A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface. Steric height—changes to sea levels driven by heat rather than melting ice—has reached the highest levels Rudnick has ever seen.

“I looked back at our data to make sure that I'm not making a mistake and it's correct—and it is,” Rudnick, who works at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego, says.

According to recent reports, in Monterey Bay, a station recorded a temperature of 64.72 degrees Fahrenheit (18.18 degrees Celsius) at a depth of 200 feet below the water’s surface in late October, breaking previous records. Other data shows even hotter water in San Diego at the same depth: 77 degrees Fahrenheit, an anomaly of 21.3 degrees Fahrenheit above normal.

It has been revealed that el Niño “is the biggest source of climate variability” off the California coast, Rudnick states. The climate phenomenon is characterized by hotter-than-normal water in the eastern tropical Pacific and affects weather and oceans around the globe. His gliders have captured temperature anomalies across other events, including intense heat during the 2015–2016 super El Niño. But this year’s El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record, and its impacts are equally supersized.

“It’s fair to say it’s off the charts,” he notes.

This year’s El Niño is adding heat to an already-simmering ocean. Since January 2025, coastal California waters have been hit by a massive heat wave, with temperatures in some places reaching 8 degrees Fahrenheit above average in August. Add in human-caused climate change—oceans off Southern California have warmed 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit since the 1970s alone—and it makes for unprecedented conditions now.

In a recent development, “This is a bunch of things that have had to come together to make this even physically possible,” Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, notes. “And even then, it's kind of astonishing.”.

According to recent reports, rudnick agrees. “The heat we get from El Niño stacking on top of the heat we already have, that’s the thing that makes this most unusual,” he indicates.

According to recent reports, part of what’s driving the higher ocean temperatures and sea levels off California are what’s known as Kelvin waves. These slow, large waves transport warm water from west to east across the Pacific. They in turn push down the ocean’s thermocline, a transition layer into the deeper ocean where temperatures begin to decrease rapidly.

It has been revealed that “It isn't like there's some heater in the deep ocean suddenly,” Swain notes. “It's just that we've turned off the air conditioner and we're allowing the surface waters to warm.”.

Kelvin waves can also help to raise sea levels along the California coast by “keeping the water from moving physically offshore,” Swain claims. While Kelvin waves are imperceptible to the average person, their impacts aren’t.

Californians have been living through several weeks of intense coastal flooding and big waves enhanced by these higher sea levels. San Francisco and the surrounding area are under a coastal flood advisory through Friday morning, and waves have reached over 30 feet (9 meters) in height and even set off seismographs. (Another storm is set to hit the Bay Area this weekend.) It’s also contributing to heavier rainfall, with locations from San Francisco to Burbank setting hourly rainfall records in recent days.

But the warmer water itself is also contributing to this temporary sea level rise, thanks to simple physics: Warmer water takes up more space, helping push up sea levels.

The warm water is driving weather even more unprecedented than the intense storms. On Tuesday, two rare twin waterspouts formed over San Francisco Bay, the result of cold storm air moving over unusually warm waters. These phenomena are generally seen off the coast of Florida or the Mediterranean—not in the usually frigid waters of the Pacific.

“The air temperatures are somewhat winter-like right now, but the water ain't,” Swain claims. “It’s an indicator that things aren’t as they usually are in this part of the world.”.

Breaking: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising newly introduced study

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for new treatments for chronic neck and back pain.
  • In a recent development, the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine.
  • Although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer newly introduced ways to slow spinal degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for new treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

In a recent development, the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

Although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer newly introduced ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

Most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

Over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are currently available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

It has been revealed that researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

To investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden.

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

Industry observers note that as the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

Industry observers note that the researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

According to recent reports, importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A.

Industry observers note that to understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

Several unexpected connections emerged.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

Industry observers note that additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

Industry observers note that together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play important roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup.

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

The team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially notable targets for future drugs.

Sources indicate that however, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

New Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments.

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

"For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting.".

The findings could be particularly important for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

Industry observers note that dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential fresh therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

"We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered important genetic evidence that could pave the way for new treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring.".

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

Dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, said:.

"This research highlights how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing fresh knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives.".

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several fresh avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.
  • The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.

The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.

The opening price valued the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

Yet, after the first two days of trading, Anthropic stock closed Friday more than 20% below its opening price at $87.80, suggesting the hype had run ahead of what investors were willing to pay.

Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.

In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.

While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.

Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.

The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.

The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.

"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.

Dick remarked Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued.".

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation tech giant," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money.".

Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction.".

Sources indicate that "We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie.".

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

It has been revealed that with many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

In a recent development, there are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.

In a recent development, "They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs.".

Recent findings suggest that that has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to concern upcoming AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have confirmed deals worth $67 billion.

Rees stated another sign could be any latest regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

Industry observers note that when the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18, 19 and 20 to reflect the latest developments.

Tristan Thompson Reveals His “Home Run” Investment in Anthropic AI

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Noting he's “happy" about the organization's recent successes, Thompson told Yahoo Finance that he got involved in the tech brand over two years ago while visiting San Francisco as part of his NBA schedule when he was playing for the Cleveland Cavaliers.
  • Thompson—who shares kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with ex Khloe Kardashian—met up with Sriram Krishnan, now a Senior White House Policy Advisor on Artificial Intelligence, who he described as a "great buddy of mine.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tristan Thompson has made nothing but net gains.

At least, that’s true when it comes to his early investment in Anthropic AI, the artificial intelligence tech giant that saw major financial wins this week when it went public and sold $81.3 billion worth of stock shares, according to CNBC.

Noting he's “happy" about the organization's recent successes, Thompson told Yahoo Finance that he got involved in the tech brand over two years ago while visiting San Francisco as part of his NBA schedule when he was playing for the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Thompson—who shares kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with ex Khloe Kardashian—met up with Sriram Krishnan, now a Senior White House Policy Advisor on Artificial Intelligence, who he described as a "great buddy of mine.".

Sources indicate that "The only friend that I had in SF during those Finals runs that was picking the Cavaliers to win, he opened up these doors," Thompson recalled in the interview published Nov. 19. "Going to dinners and and meeting people. I think SF is one of those towns where a lot of great founders and early startups, they want to come together and build this ecosystem.".

It has been revealed that "And I mentioned, 'You know what? Let me insert myself in,'" the 35-year-old said. "I'm the tall guy walking in. I'm probably about 10 inches taller than everyone else, and [say], 'Tell me what you're working on.'".

In a recent development, now, years after becoming an investor, Thompson explained how thrilled they were last month when Anthropic declared it had filed a proposed stock plan with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

"We're in a group chat and everyone's just talking about what they're going to do to celebrate," Thompson shared. "I remarked, 'Guys, the one thing we have to do is do a dinner. We got to break bread again.'".

As he put it, "Cheers to getting it right this time.".

Because, as the Miami Heat player admitted, his ventures don't always pay off like Anthropic did, breaking records with its initial public offering (CNBC reported it had a fully diluted market cap of about $1.8 trillion on Nov. 19).

"Listen, out of 10 companies you invest in, you're lucky if two make it to the finish line and get the home run," Thompson explained. "But what I tell people is those two that make it to the finish line and win that championship in their eyes for what the company's trying to do, it will make up for all the capital that you invested in.".

According to recent reports, as for whether he aims to cash out of Anthropic? Not so fast—he sees himself as a long-term shareholder.

"I'm extremely bullish," Thompson added. "Their alignment with government definitely makes you feel very bullish about it. It's almost like investing in Google during the dot com era.".

For more stars getting candid on their finances and paychecks, read on.

Sources indicate that (E! and CNBC are both part of Versant Media.).

The Jackass star reflected on the "comical" amount of money he was paid for doing death-defying stunts on the MTV series' first season in 2000.

Sources indicate that "When it was all stated and done, after taxes, I was paid less than $1,500 for the entire first season of Jackass," the daredevil told Playboy in June 2026. "Before the show came out, my sister kicked me out of the house. I was broke, unemployed, and homeless, and a star on this major MTV show.".

Industry observers note that oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence was paid $25 million to star in Adam McKay’s ensemble disaster comedy Don’t Look Up. But her costar and fellow Oscar winner Leonardo DiCaprio got $30 million.

Recent findings suggest that “Look, Leo brings in more box office than I do,” Lawrence told Vanity Fair for its’ December 2020/January 2021 glitch. “I’m extremely fortunate and happy with my deal. But in other situations, what I have seen—and I’m sure other women in the workforce have seen as well—is that it’s extremely uncomfortable to inquire about equal pay. And if you do question something that appears unequal, you’re told it’s not gender disparity but they can’t tell you what exactly it is.”.

Her sanguine attitude was hard-fought: When the disparity between Lawrence’s compensation and that of her male costars for 2013’s American Hustle was revealed in the 2014 Sony email hack, it prompted an industry-wide conversation about the gender pay gap in Hollywood.

"I'm so fortunate to have my job. My problem is not money," Lawrence told the U.K.’s Channel 4 News in 2017. "I wasn't upset that I only got this many millions for a movie. That's ridiculous. I was angry about the unfairness and inequality.".

The *NSYNC alum revealed that he and his fellow bandmates JC Chasez, Joey Fatone, Chris Kirkpatrick and Justin Timberlake didn't make much money during their years with the group.

Industry observers note that “We had a per diem: $35 a day,” he revealed on The Zach Sang Show in 2026. “Our first check was a $10,000 check after years of No. 1 albums, sellout tours. I don’t know how many millions they made off of merchandise because merchandise was insane.”.

“And then they finally gave us a check for $10,000,” he recalled. “You’re like, ‘Oh, thanks.’ We should be grateful for that, been working for free for two, three years now.”.

Less comparable to DiCaprio’s salary: The $60,000 “before commissions and taxes” that Jonah Hill was paid for 2013’s The Wolf of Wall Street, while the titular wolf made $10 million.

Industry observers note that “They gave me the lowest amount of money possible,” Hill recalled on The Howard Stern Show in 2014. But it was the chance to appear in a Martin Scorsese movie, so the Moneyball alum wanted to get the deal done before anyone could change their mind.

Sources indicate that “I would sell my house and give him all my money to work for [Scorsese],” explained Hill, who earned his second Best Supporting Actor nomination for his turn as a squirrelly substance-abusing stockbroker. “This isn't what you make money for. You do 22 Jump Street or you do other things, and you can pay your rent. I would have done anything in the world. I would do it again in a second. This isn't about money. You should do things that you care about.".

According to Dylan Sprouse, his residuals from filming The Suite Life of Zack & Cody with twin brother Cole Sprouse is anything but suite.

According to recent reports, "The only residual check I've ever received for The Suite Life at all was a crossover episode with Hannah Montana for five cents," the Disney Channel alum shared during a 2026 episode of his Wildmen podcast. "In a time where residuals would have been great, not a single paycheck for being arguably one of the most popular shows on television.".

Industry observers note that while there's no cash prize for nabbing Dancing With the Stars' mirrorball trophy, “whoever makes it to the finale, you all get paid up until then," Jenna Johnson, who won season 33 with partner Joey Graziadei, shared. "And you do get a nice bonus.”.

In a recent development, "If you win," Johnson, who noted pro contracts are dependent on seniority, continued. "it’s not like you get a million dollars. You’re just getting a cute trophy together.” As for those who say farewell to the ballroom early, well, as she explained, "You’re guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks.” According to multiple reports, dancer salaries start at around $1,200 to $1,600 an episode, which can increase to up to of $100,000 per season. (ABC has not confirmed these reports.) On the flip side, celebrities receive a starting salary of $125,000. As they cha-cha further into the competition, stars  receive additional bonuses with the semifinalists and finalists getting paid up to $50,000 extra.

The actress seemingly confirmed that the Friends cast—including Jennifer Aniston, Courtney Cox,David Schwimmer and Matt LeBlanc—get $20 million in residuals per year from the show re-airing, quipping to The Times in April 2026 that if she had to guess why, it's “Because Phoebe Buffay was so great?".

But in actuality, she praised the talents of her costars for their performances.

“I felt I did OK, but Jennifer and Courteney? Amazing,” she raved. “David and Matt? They had me laughing so hard. And then Matthew [Perry]—he was just beyond us all.”.

According to recent reports, to hear Joe Giudice tell it, his and ex-wife Teresa Giudice's salary for season one of The Real Housewives of New Jersey was nothing to flip over. "We got paid nothing the first season," he detailed on daughter Gia Giudice's Casual Chaos podcast in August 2025. "I'll even say, it was like $25,000. It was ridiculous. But, whatever.".

In a recent development, and the ingredientses they put into that initial fame-making season weren't cheap. "I think the first year we had that big party in my great room," the father of four reflected. "I think that show cost me $150,000 the first year.".

Oprah Winfrey happily accepted only a little bit of green to star in 1985’s The Color Purple.

Sources indicate that “They were only offering $35,000 to be in this film, and it is the best $35,000 I ever earned,” the billionaire media mogul told Essence in 2023. “It changed everything and taught me so much.”.

The actress revealed that she made about $20,000 per episode of Two and a Half Men with a 5 percent raise each season, making about $43,000 for one episode in the final season.

When she scored the role of late Tejana singer Selena Quintanilla in the 1997 biopic Selena, Jennifer Lopez became the first Latina actress to earn $1 million for a film.

“I was too young and didn’t know what the hell was going on,” Lopez told Variety in 2019, reflecting on her breakout movie. “It was great they offered me a million dollars. I feel like everyone was making a statement.”.

And it paved the way for her to make hundreds of millions more, though sometimes her participation doesn’t cost a thing.

Sources indicate that “I do things because I love them,” Lopez explained to GQ in 2019. “I didn't get paid a whole bunch of money for Hustlers. I did it for free and produced it. I bank on myself, you know? Like Jenny From the Block—I do what I love.".

Recent findings suggest that adrien Brody didn’t do The Brutalist for the money. Rather, he took on the role of a Hungarian architect suffering for his art in post-WWII America for $250,000 and won his second Oscar for Best Actor.

“I need a studio movie now, because I’ve poured it all into this,” Brody quipped to Variety, referring to the “barn that looks like a castle” he’s renovating in upstate Newly introduced York.

In a recent development, “Do you guys know what they pay us?” Pete Davidson cracked to Fresh York magazine when asked ahead of Saturday Night Live's 50th anniversary special how he spent his money when he was first hired at the age of 20 in 2014. “It’s like three grand an episode, so I think I got dinner.”.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, the salaries have remained proportional for SNL newcomers, with season one stars John Belushi, Jane Curtin, Gilda Radner, Dan Aykroyd and Chevy Chase reportedly earning $750 an episode back in 1975. Which was roughly equivalent to $3,300 in 2014, according to the Consumer Price Index Inflation calculator. (Though the $750 of 1975 is $4,428 in 2025.).

While Kenan Thompson makes a lot more than $3,000 per episode of SNL now that he’s in his record 22nd season, the former Nickelodeon star had to start somewhere.

It has been revealed that “That first commercial when they paid me, it was $800,” the All That alum revealed in Demi Lovato‘s 2024 documentary Child Star. “I was 12 so that may as well have been a million dollars.".

It turns out Gilmore Girls’ status as a beloved rewatchable classic is literally priceless.

“There really are no residuals on Netflix,” Lauren Graham, who played Lorelai Gilmore for seven seasons and then reprised the role for 2016’s Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life, said on Jimmy Kimmel Live in March 2025. “But I’ve been paid in love and appreciation.”.

Feeling not so appreciated, Tommy Dorfman got specific about her 13 Reasons Why paycheck during the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike—which was prompted in part (as was the WGA strike) by streamers like Netflix not making it a practice to pay additional compensation to cast and crew once a show had become a big hit.

Industry observers note that "my earnings for the entire first season of 13 reasons why were $29,953.24 prior to agency and manager fees (20%) and taxes," Dorfman wrote on Threads July 24. "8 episodes over six months." She continued, “i did all of the promo and had KEY ART for this show, flew round trip from NYC to SF to shoot for every episode, was kept for days without pay/working. i barely qualified for insurance.".

In a recent development, and, Dorfman added, “within the first 28 days of release, the show's season 1 garnered a total of 476 million view hours. this is why we strike.".

Without naming names or numbers, Dax Shepard told fellow Parenthood alum Lauren Graham when she appeared on his podcast that he knew he made “among the lowest of all the actors” on their NBC drama, which ran for six seasons.

But, the Armchair Expert host stressed that he did not mind.

“Every job I had ever had in my life prior to Parenthood, I made a point to find out what everyone was making,” he said. “I'd always figure it out—either a conversation where I get it out of them or I backchannel through an agent.".

So he made a point to purposely not seek out such info about his Parenthood family, which helped with enjoying the experience even when he did get an inkling of where he was on the pay pyramid.

It has been revealed that “I got a dollar for writing the script,” George Clooney told the Los Angeles Times in 2005 about the financial strings he pulled to get his film Good Night, and Good Luck made. “I had to endorse my check for directing and turn in my acting salary. [Actor, cowriter and coproducer Grant Heslov] and I each made a buck for doing it.”.

Sources indicate that his labor of love about CBS News journalist Edward R. Murrow speaking truth to power in the 1950s had legs, though: Making his Broadway debut, Clooney wrapped his months-long stint playing Murrow in a stage adaptation of the film  in June 2025. And with the play having grossed a Broadway record (for a nonmusical) $3.3 million during a preview week before it officially opened April 3, he made a lot more than $1.

For his chilling turn as Patrick Bateman in 2000’s American Psycho, Christian Bale was paid “the absolute minimum they were legally allowed to pay me” because no one in the production really wanted to hire him except director Mary Harron, the Welsh actor told GQ in 2022.

He made so little, Bale shared, that he remembered “sitting in the makeup trailer and the makeup artists were laughing at me because I was getting paid less than any of them.”.

No, the Game of Thrones cast didn't get paid $300,000 per episode, according to Emilia Clarke.

“We didn’t earn that much," she told Variety in 2026. "Can you imagine? I’d have been driving a couple of Porsches!".

However, the actress—who played Daenerys Targaryen for eight seasons between 2011 and 2019—noted that the money she made throughout the HBO show did provide her with enough financial security to pay off her parents’ mortgage.

His uncle may have been Rico, but Jon Heder confirmed in 2010 that he was “initially” only paid $1,000 for Napoleon Dynamite.

After the irreverent comedy became a sleeper hit, he was able to renegotiate for a piece of the profits, telling the New Zealand Herald, “They went a little bit higher.”.

Djimon Hounsou said he’s “definitely underpaid” in Hollywood despite his prestigious list of credits, including Amistad and Blood Diamond.

Industry observers note that "I've been in this business and making films now over two decades," the Beninese actor told CNN’s Larry Madowo in January 2025. "And still—with two Oscar nominations and been in many big blockbuster films—and yet I’m still struggling financially to make a living.".

Rebel Wilson detailed in her 2024 memoir Rebel Rising that she was paid $3,500 to do Bridesmaids, “a fee that I then had to pay directly to the Screen Actors Guild to join the union. So really, I got paid nothing.”.

Still, she wrote, the experience was “everything!”.

And the Australian actress’ star rose ever a-ca higher, with her fee going from the SAG minimum scale of $65,000 for 2012’s Pitch Perfect to $10 million for 2017’s Pitch Perfect 3. Wilson wrote that she raked in $20 million total for the threequel, Isn’t It Romantic and The Hustle, though—reality alert—she “lost almost 50 percent to taxes, 10 percent to agents and 5 percent” to her lawyer. But even after those obligations and paying her publicist, business manager and assistant, Wilson “netted what to me was an absolute fortune.”.

In late 2017, Ellen Pompeo negotiated a newly introduced Grey’s Anatomy contract for $575,000 per episode, a seven-figure signing bonus and two full backend equity points worth an estimated $6 million to $7 million.

According to recent reports, “I’m 48 now, so I’ve finally gotten to the place where I’m OK asking for what I deserve, which is something that comes only with age,” Pompeo told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018. “Because I’m not the most ‘relevant’ actress out there. I know that’s the industry perception because I’ve been this character for 14 years. But the truth is, anybody can be good on a show season one and two. Can you be good 14 years later? Now, that’s a f--kin’ skill.”.

Reflecting more recently on how she always made less than costar Patrick Dempsey, even though she was the Grey in question, Pompeo mentioned she didn’t begrudge him his money.

It has been revealed that but, she mentioned on a March 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy, “Just being that I was the namesake of the show, I deserved the same and that was harder to get. I wasn't salty about him getting what he got. I was salty that they didn't value me as much as they valued him and they never will.”.

Jamie Lee Curtis recalled getting paid $2,000 a week—so $8,000 in total—for 1978’s Halloween, her movie debut. “I mean,” she told Rotten Tomatoes in 2018, “nobody got paid, anything.”.

Yet while the scream queen earned four figures, director John Carpenter’s friend Nick Castle felt like a king making $25 per day to share the role of Michael Myers. (It’s Anthony Moran whose face you see when the killer’s mask comes off for a freaky second, and editor Tommy Lee Wallace also logged screentime as Michael.).

Industry observers note that “That was a lot at the time!” Castle, who attended film school at USC with Carpenter, told Vanity Fair in 2018. “You have to remember: My interest in doing the film was being on set, so I could demystify the experience of filmmaking and directing. I expected to hang around the set for no money. But hey, $25 per day, and all I had to do was wear a rubber mask.”.

Sources indicate that taraji P. Henson earned a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination for 2008’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, but years later she was still fired up by the $150,000 she accepted to be in the movie—after producers rejected the $500,000 quote she brought to the table.

As for the film’s leads Brad Pitt and Cate Blanchett, “You don’t hear a lot of $20 million quotes anymore, but at this time that was happening,” Henson said on the Ladies First With Laura Brown podcast in 2021. “And rightfully so—I’m not saying they shouldn’t have paid Cate and Brad what they deserved.”.

Industry observers note that but, she continued, “I’m bringing a certain amount to the seat too and I felt like what I was asking at that time in my career was fair, was fair to the ticket sales that I would contribute to this big film. Wouldn’t do it.” Henson was “gutted” when they offered $100,000, she recalled. “When it was all mentioned and done I got $150,000, but I had to swallow my pride, baby.”.

Breaking it down, “I know people go, ‘$150,000, that’s a lot of money!’” Henson acknowledged. “I don’t ever want people to think that I’m ungrateful because that is not me.” But, she calculated, “Uncle Sam is going to take 50 percent of that, so now you’re left with, what? $75,000. Now before Uncle Sam takes the money, I have to pay my team before taxes, 30 percent. So once Uncle Sam takes his 75, then I got another 30 that’s coming off of that 75, so I may have made $40,000?”.

While Blanchett has made plenty of money over the years, it didn’t all come from playing royal elf Galadriel in The Lord of the Rings franchise, though it grossed $2.9 billion at the worldwide box office.

According to recent reports, “Are you kidding me? No,” she retorted on Watch What Happens Live in August 2024 when Andy Cohen guessed LOTR was her biggest paycheck. “No one got paid anything to do that movie…I mean, I basically got free sandwiches, and I got to keep my ears.”.

They weren’t paid a precious amount, that is. Orlando Bloom, who played elven warrior Legolas, shared on The Howard Stern Show in 2023 that he made $175,000 for the whole trilogy.

Hopefully he also got to keep his ears.

Yellowjackets Season 4: What clues are hiding in the opening credits?

  • In a recent development, the theme song, "No Return" by Craig Wedren and Anna Waronker, roars to life over VHS footage once more.
  • In Season 4, Episode 1, here are all the curious images we noticed:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that yellowjackets is back. With Season 4 comes latest mysteries and new opening title cards inviting viewers to speculate on what's next. With each episode, Mashable will be probing these details, looking for questions and their answers. So, buckle up.

In a recent development, the theme song, "No Return" by Craig Wedren and Anna Waronker, roars to life over VHS footage once more. Some images are classic, like pre-crash footage of the team smiling and Jackie (Ella Purnell) smirking on the soccer pitch and drawing a threatening finger across her neck. But others are new.

In Season 4, Episode 1, here are all the curious images we noticed:.

Melanie Lynskey is shown wide-mouthed before a microphone, suggesting adult Shauna has something to say (or sing?) in Season 4. Considering Shauna has a special skill for brutal one-liners, whoever she's looking at should be trembling.

Under blood and a prosthetic broken nose, Sophie Nélisse is hard to recognize in the moment. But freeze-frame the credits, and there's no doubt that's Teen Shauna. She's lying in the snow. So, presumably this is still when the girls were in the wilderness.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of the Season 3, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) successfully reached the outside world through the frog scientist's SAT phone. So, what happens before rescue comes?

#105096. Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1137 w)
